utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I do understand that the Defence wishes to interrupt the testimony of Mr. Rajak and to first start hearing Mr. Banduka's evidence. And that meets no objections --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, could the next witness, which is Mr. Banduka, be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the time to put on the record that the Prosecution has advised the Chamber that it has received the B/C/S translation for P06715, 65 ter 31183, MFI'd through witness Milenko Indjic on the 3rd of September, 2014, and it was MFI'd pending translation. This is -- I've not verified it but I rely on the information provided by the Prosecution. We can see it at transcript page 25188. The translation, as we understand, has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID R014-9738-BCS. And if the Defence agrees, the Prosecution requests that the court officer be instructed to attach the translation and that the document be admitted. P6715 is admitted into evidence. If there are any reasons to revisit the issue of the translation, then the Chamber would like to hear within the next 48 hours. Yes, before I admit it, I first should have instructed Mr. Registrar to attach the translation of which I gave the details a second ago, to attach the translation to the original in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Banduka, I presume. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka, please be seated. Mr. Banduka, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, for the record, tell us your name but slowly.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Rajko Banduka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, did you give a statement to the Mladic Defence team, to me, to be more precise? You provided a written statement answering the questions that were put to you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 1D01745.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, you have a text in front of you. It's in B/C/S. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether the information in this part of the text is correct and also whether the signature on this page is your signature.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you have it before you. Again, the same question,

utterances.speaker: MR. BANDUKA
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose signature this is and whether the date was entered in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today when you entered the courtroom and when you made the solemn declaration to tell the truth, would you answer the questions that were put to you in the same way as is recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is the right moment to tender Mr. Rajko Banduka's statement. The 65 ter number is 1D01745. I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Prosecution, but I don't know whom to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D711 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read a summary of Mr. Rajko Banduka's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Rajko Banduka is a professional soldier, a career soldier. When the war started he was in Sarajevo. He was the aide-de-camp of the command of the 2nd Military District of the JNA. When the war broke out, he was arrested when a JNA column was leaving Sarajevo. When he was released from prison, he was moved to the Han Pijesak garrison. Over there, he became the aide-de-camp of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He has remained in that position until the end of the war. He will testify about the setting up of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, about the capabilities of the Main Staff in terms of personnel and equipment, on the communications means used by General Mladic while he was at Crna Rijeka facility. He is -- he will also testify the functioning and the organisation of work of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, as well as of his specific tasks and his relationship with General Mladic. He will describe in detail the communication system which was housed in the facility where General Mladic stayed in Crna Rijeka. He will also speak about the process of decision-making at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He is familiar with the way of work and the attitude of General Mladic towards subordinated officers. He particularly emphasises his military and professional attitude towards the civilian population. He says that there was no desire on his behalf to retaliate against the enemy side even under the most difficult circumstances. He also speaks about the attitude of General Mladic towards paramilitary groups and his desire to extend assistance to everybody irrespective of their ethnic affiliations. He also speaks about his own tasks and duties at the moment when General Mladic was not at the Crna Rijeka facility. He also says that Mr. Mladic, as the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, spent a lot of his time on the front lines amongst his people and soldiers. He also underscores all of his human and moral values and character traits. Your Honour, this was a short summary of this witness's statement. With your leave, I would have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put questions to the witness, Mr. Stojanovic, preferably about facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I would like to call up 711. D711, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, Mr. Banduka, you will see one part of your statement. In paragraph 2, you say that you bear witness to an agreement between the then-president, Alija Izetbegovic; General Milutin Kukanjac; the UNPROFOR commander, General MacKenzie; the head of the European Monitoring Mission, Colm Doyle; and others, regarding the peaceful retreat and passage of a JNA column towards Lukavac. Please explain to the Trial Chamber what you mean when you say that you bore witness to those agreements? What did you personally see and hear? Please stick to the facts.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was physically present in the meeting room after President Izetbegovic arrived from Lukavica. The room was General Kukanjac's office, where Mr. Izetbegovic had a cup of coffee. He was accompanied by Mr. Zlatko Lagumdzija and his daughter, and they were joined with other highly ranked officials of the then-MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that room there were also high-ranking officers of the then-JNA, including the commander of the 2nd Military District. There was a request made that the movement of the column should be delayed by another 15 or 20 minutes, which would have allowed the column to be properly formed, for all the stuff to be loaded onto the vehicles. I was physically present there when that was happening. I saw the sentiment of all the participants in that meeting. I realised that things would go smoothly, in a dignified manner. I believe that that would be the case. After that coffee break, we went out to the courtyard of the command of the 2nd Military District. President Izetbegovic and General MacKenzie shook hands with the soldiers. They were observing them packing and leaving, and then they decided to leave. That was the first piece of information I had about the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- is there any dispute about the agreement having been concluded and is there any issue taken by the Prosecution about who were present when this agreement was signed or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't have a dispute at this point, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whether something could arise in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you never know. Mr. Stojanovic, there seems to be at this moment neither about the existence nor about -- at this moment about the agreement dealing with matters as described. That's the withdrawal. So, therefore, why then ask whether we -- the participants had coffee or tea or water to drink. It's irrelevant and there's no dispute. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you gain an impression about the fact whether Alija Izetbegovic was in control of the situation, whether he could have any influence on the departure of the column?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic himself offered that he would come and that he would escort the column from the command of the 2nd Military District to Lukavica. It had been agreed that he would get into another vehicle on the Skenderija bridge, that he would go to the Presidency building, and then eventually he would meet General Kukanjac in Nedzarici after the column arrived Lukavica. I saw concern on his face. I was not sure that he was really in control of the whole situation, irrespective of the fact that he was physically present and that he had made all the promises that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at paragraph 5 in your statement. In it you say that the Main Staff was set up and that personnel arrived in the command, and then the system of communications was set up and allowed you to have a direct protected connection with the corps commanders and the commander of the air force. In view of your military education, could you please tell the Court what kind of communication system did you have at the facility where General Mladic stayed when he was in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we just could get a time-frame, it would take some of the vagueness out of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you accommodate the concerns expressed by -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, the suggestion was understandable and in view of that, can you please explain: When you say when the Main Staff was set up, when was that? Do you mean that this answer is relative to the first year of the functioning of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: The communication system that I had and that was exclusively used by General Mladic for his command functions was an interphone. By pressing on a button he could communicate directly with his subordinated units, and those were the corps and the air force. That connection was protected, it was encrypted, which means that one of the direct participants was the commander of the Main Staff and the other participant was the corps commander. Besides those encrypted and protected connections there were other means of communications but they were not protected and they were provided from the local switchboard. There were numbers attached to those lines and those lines could be used in communication with other protagonists of the communication system. In addition to that, we also had two civilian numbers, as it were, which were used in communication with the telephone numbers abroad and other people, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, still the place - and that's what you started asking about - and the time is still unclear. What you just told us, was that the situation in Crna Rijeka? Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I will answer. That facility was where I and General Mladic stayed. It was separated from the Main Staff and the Main Staff was where the interphone was and from there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, before you tell us whether it was at the corner or at a place or whatever, my question was: Was that in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Crna Rijeka. At the facility where General Mladic stayed, where he was billeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From when to when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the first day of 1992, from the 9th of May until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those telephone lines that you spoke about and those communications means that you referred to, could they be intercepted by the enemy side from other territories and from other states?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Those direct lines with the commanders and the air force commander could not be intercepted because they were encrypted, while the civilian lines, the switchboard numbers and the participants who communicated via those numbers, their conversations could be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Regular combat reports, interim combat reports that subordinated units submitted to the Main Staff of the VRS, where did they end up? Where did they arrive physically?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Every written piece of information was encrypted. Telegrams were sent and arrived at the encryption station at the communications centre. It was received by a person who processed or, rather, opened that information, as we say. He would then pack it into an envelope and handed it over to the operative centre of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the functions and you -- you had and duties you performed throughout the war, could you tell us whether General Mladic was ever in a situation or was he in a situation to receive those daily combat reports from subordinated units every day, did they arrive at his desk every day?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. Things did not transpire that way. General Mladic and myself did not receive that information. That information did not reach me. That information ended up in the operative centre and at the staff which was a kilometre to 2 kilometres away from us. The reason for that was that General Mladic did not spend a lot of time in Crna Rijeka [as interpreted]. He was in the units and in the field. As for the information and its contents, if he was there, he would be conveyed that information from the operative centre of the Main Staff or the Chief of Staff himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just been told that on page 10, line 11 -- no, page 11, line 3, I'm sorry, Your Honours, it says "Crna Rijeka."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain this? In response to this question, did you say that when General Mladic was not in Crna Rijeka or when he was not with you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: You really have to clarify this for me. I don't know what you actually mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, when responding to my question, you said where regular and interim combat reports arrived, those coming from subordinate units. And then you went on and you said that at moments when General Mladic was not, and so on and so forth. I have no other way of asking you. When he was not where?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Regardless of whether he is with me in the room, the telegrams did not end up with us. Rather, telegrams waited for him at the operation centre in Crna Rijeka or with the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka. At this point in time, we have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Before the Prosecution will cross-examine you, Judge Fluegge first has a question for you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just one additional question to paragraph 2 which was dealt with by Mr. Stojanovic. You are talking about two different matters in paragraph 2. First, your capture, your imprisonment by Green Berets and Patriotic League. When have you been released from that detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 3rd of May, I was taken prisoner during the notorious Dobrovoljacka Street affair and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please listen to my question. I wanted to know when you were released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 6th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you were in detention for three days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The second matter you dealt with in paragraph 2 is the meeting of Mr. Izetbegovic and General MacKenzie. When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not speak about a meeting. I spoke about the arrival of General MacKenzie and President Alija Izetbegovic on the 3rd of May, with the motive as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you -- I'm not asking you about any motive. You stated in your statement: "I witnessed the agreements between the then-president, Alija Izetbegovic, General Kukanjac, and to the UNPROFOR commander, General MacKenzie, and others." When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 3rd of May, around 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means on the same day when you were captured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. You find him to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your rank in 1992 and throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: I was a warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's under a lieutenant. It's not a commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's stay with your statement at D711.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this -- looking at paragraph 4 - it's also page 2 in the B/C/S - you describe that General Mladic -- that the conditions in which he was throughout the war were very modest and that it was more important for him that the people in the army had better conditions than him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to 65 ter 31502.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: This is the facility where General Mladic and I were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is located in Crna Rijeka at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes. It is about a kilometre and a half or two away from the other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is known as the Villa Javor?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is right near the entrance to the underground bunker that goes under the hill?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this the modest accommodation you're speaking of in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 3 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Both languages. That's the same D711. Same thing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in looking at paragraph 7, if we look at the bottom of paragraph 7 you say: "My conclusion is that he never reached decisions or wrote orders on his own but with the help of and after a joint analysis with the staff and the operations centre." You've also said today that he communicated with his corps commanders. So I take it his corps commanders were part of that joint decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: You did not put a good question to me. Not from there. Not from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were his corps commanders someone that he listened to in making his decisions, as far as you know, being the communication facilitator that you have described?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, he would hear what they had to say, but over the telephone, conversations were very brief, without going into any kind of detail or without issuing any kind of orders. For the most part, this was done in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You knew those -- some of those conversations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you said, Witness: "For the most part, this was done in writing." What was done in writing for the most part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orders, directives -- actually, orders and everything else that was derived from that. That was created in the staff or the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The issue discussed and asked about was the input of the corps commanders, not about in what way decisions or orders were communicated. That's why I was confused about "this was done in writing." Would you say that brief telephone conversations were the exclusive source of input by the corps commanders, which assisted General Mladic in preparing his decisions? Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it can be put that way, but not entirely. Why am I saying that? Because corps commanders did not present details over that telephone. It was just an opportunity to talk and to give him brief answers to questions that he put. I could not formulate that because I didn't even listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer the picture of the villa, 65 ter 31502, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6848 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the operations centre you spoke of that was -- it was down the hill from the villa some distance. What was the distance again?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: As the crow flies, perhaps not even 6- to 800 metres, but the road that led there is about 1.2 to 1.5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in times where there was security concerns, such as NATO bombing or attacks from the enemy, did Mladic and his command staff have the ability to move into the bunker and carry on the operations centre and communications from the bunker?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible. And that did happen during the bombing, that briefly we went to that command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the area where the operations centre was down the hill, or a distance that you've described, that was two narrow wooden buildings next to each other where the offices of the staff and the assistant commanders were?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's where the Chief of Staff and deputy commander, General Milovanovic, had an office?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mladic also had an office there that he could use when he was in the mood to leave the villa.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, he did not have an office. But he used the office of the Chief of Staff or the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in 1992, who was the chief of operations and training that you spoke of when you referred to the combat reports?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember the name right now, who it could have been in 1992. If it wasn't General Miletic, then I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In 1995, at least you know it was General Radoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your statement, on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 4. B/C/S, both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You talk about getting seriously ill in May of 1995 and that you were hospitalised in Belgrade until 26 May 1995. And that you were -- and I quote: "I was able to observe all the events surrounding Srebrenica and Zepa only on TV." And where were you watching the Srebrenica and Zepa events on TV? Where were you then?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: I was in my apartment in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you go back and start working again for the VRS and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Because of illness, I had been declared unfit for a longer period of time. The hospital of the Main Staff granted me 90 days of sick-leave. However, during the first half of August 1995, I came to visit them at my own initiative, and that's how I stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you start up work again the first half of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It could have been the first week of August 1995, couldn't it have been?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly. I don't remember the date. I was not fit to work, but I was physically present, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you -- had you come down with hemorrhagic fever?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one of the symptoms of that is the difficulty in urinating?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 31493.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you've told us, you knew that you were being listened to by the enemies. You haven't testified here before, have you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you told or were you aware that the Prosecution had many intercepts of -- from the Muslims and the Croatians before testifying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems me that perhaps this document should not be broadcast to the public in view of our practice to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not to be shown to the public. And to the extent it has been done already, to be redacted. It has not been done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see that this is from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 2nd Corps command. It's dated the 3rd of August, 1995. And let's go to the next page in both languages. It's page 2 in the B/C/S; 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we could see from the initial page that this was a conversation between a Dr. Zale and a Rajko Banduka. Did you know a Dr. Zale?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Dr. Zale, no; but Dr. Zdrale, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. For that correction of my bad pronunciation and the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can see, as you look at this, that the doctor is just calling to ask you about your health and you say that you had hemorrhagic fever. And the doctor asks if you were blocked from urinating, and you said yes. And we see down near the bottom of it that when the doctor asks you: "Good. Any aftermaths?" And you say: "So far no. The medical board gave me another three months and I am back to work now. I feel all right most of the time." So is this a real conversation, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does this help refresh your recollection you were actually back at work at least on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: I've already said that physically I was probably there and that I probably spoke to friends on the phone. But that I was completely capable of working, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you told this doctor you were back at work. Were you not being honest with him?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what else I could have answered. As soon as he heard my voice, I said to him that I was back at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this 65 ter 31493 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6849, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Banduka, as I've read from your statement in paragraph 14, you state and you've clarified here that you were not in Crna Rijeka during Zepa or Srebrenica. You were in Bijeljina. It's the Prosecution's position, sir, that during the Zepa operation, which was in July, the period of July 13th through the 19th, when the population was bust out on 25th and 26th and the fighting continued beyond that, that you were as early as 19 July working at your post in Crna Rijeka. And I have some intercepts to show you, so I want you to think very carefully before asking -- before answering my question. Now that you think about it, sir, were you not, in fact, working during the Zepa operation in Crna Rijeka for your commander?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No. I state with full responsibility that I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- were you in Crna Rijeka at all, working or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not in Crna Rijeka physically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said that you state with follow responsibility. Is that something -- is that a statement that you received in some sort of training with the JNA? I've just heard this repeatedly in this courtroom and I'm just wondering is this something that is part of the training?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: I don't understand that question. I don't understand what you're asking me. It's a normal word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 27547.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, sometimes when the Muslim police or army were intercepting, they would summarise intercepts, and I'm about to show you a summary of an intercept that is dated, as you can see in the Serbian, 22 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to have it under seal, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, there is because I see at the bottom there is -- so we should -- it not -- not broadcast it. Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could have the English for the -- for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. McCloskey, the English has not been attached as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ah. We will endeavour to attach it. But in the meantime, I think we can all see that this is dated 22 July. And the first paragraph talks about the -- that they registered three calls from General Gobillard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The English is on the screen as well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was looking for Mladic, and Mladic was in the field and would be back. Then the next paragraph says: "We registered quite a few calls where members of the aggressing army were looking for Mladic. While talking to them, Rajko Banduka, an officer in the VRS Main Staff, said that Mladic was away and that he was doing his job which was going slowly, but, still, it's progressing and it would soon be done." And the intercept folks said that you meant Zepa. Does this help -- help you, were you fielding calls about General Mladic on this date, 22 July?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I was not fielding calls and I simply cannot link myself to this statement and this intercept. Otherwise, if you wish, I can provide a further explanation. All of these people who could listen to that phone, they identified the phone with me, but I was not there physically. So this is just a pure formality, that everything that happened on that frequency and that was intercepted was identified with me. I would be replaced by the courier, by the operator there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6850, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6850 is admitted, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for a break. However, I would have one very small question. You said that you were replaced by the courier, operator there, and so on. Would that mean that if they received a call that they would say, "This is Banduka speaking"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they wouldn't say that. But all the participants who call often would think that it was I who was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did they introduce themselves, if not by, "This is Banduka speaking"? Would they do it by their own names or by their function or by their location? What would they do which makes you believe that everyone would think it was Banduka speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, usually, and that is according to the rules actually, that names and surnames are not mentioned during our telephone conversations. Rather, it is a number or the code for the participant in the conversation. Whereas these people who knew me probably thought that I was the only one who was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break. Could you please follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in terms of time, are we on schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's taken a little bit longer and given some of his answers, I probably I'm -- Ms. Stewart tells me I have five more minutes. I would probably need an additional five or ten after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that stays within acceptable limits. We take a break and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Banduka, on the same subject I want to show you an intercept, it's P1384. And this is from the CSB or state security of Tuzla, Bosnian MUP, as you know. And this is dated the 19th of July, 1995. And we have heard evidence in this Court that sometimes the intercept operators were only able to hear one side of a conversation, and that's the case in this particular intercept. You can see that the CSB has described a telephone operator as Banduka saying: "That number isn't operational so I had to reach you like, this, contact me to the boss's house. Come on. Yes, yes." Then we look at the rest of it, and it's General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're recording as quoting "contact" whereas it reads "connect."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that fixing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we look at the rest of it, we just hear General Mladic's side of the conversation, ending with: "Zepa has surrendered." Now when you contact Mladic to someone, do you stay on the line and listen in?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you working on the 19th of July when this intercept lists a person named Banduka as taking part?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, where does it say so exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it's the telephone operator where it says: "Banduka, that number isn't operational so I had to reach you like this. Connect me to the boss's house." This is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, due does that mean that Banduka participated in that conversation or that the usual avenue, that is, through Banduka, was not operational at that point in time and that therefore they had to reach Mladic by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It wouldn't be fair to say he participated in the conversation. He participated in the initialisation of the conversation would be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, even that, I don't know whether I could repeat that for you reading this, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the -- the position of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- this is him taking the call and getting the phone to General Mladic, which is what his job was apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether the -- what this paragraph means, as a matter of fact, and let's leave it to that at this moment. Whether it means that the connection was established through Banduka or whether the connection was not established through Banduka, I think both interpretations ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course, it's up for the Trial Chamber to evaluate this. I did want to give the witness the view of the Prosecution and to the Chamber so you knew where I was going from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you presented it as -- as reality, where you didn't said [sic]: The Prosecution understands this as being this and this and this. But let's -- let's move on. The matter appears to be at least that there is an issue which may need further discussion, that has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, I think there's a difference in the B/C/S and in the English version insofar as after the name Banduka in the English version, there's a comma but not in the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a difference --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- to understand the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you very much for that. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- the witness said that -- I think he has answered the question or hasn't he? Let me just have a look. Yes, the witness has answered the question, that he was not working on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Banduka, this Chamber has also heard evidence that the Croatian government was also intercepting your VRS and RS transmissions, and in that regard, I want to show you another intercept, which is 65 ter 22185. And this also should be noted as occurring on the 19th of July. This one at 2059 hours. The last one we saw was noted by Muslim state security as 2100 hours. And we'll see that when it comes up. And in this conversation, it appears the Croats were able to get a bit more of the conversation in the opinion of the Prosecution. So please take a look at this. It also identifies this as a transcript between General Mladic, first on the telephone is his secretary, Warrant Officer Second Class Rajko Banduka. You've told us you were a warrant officer. Did the Croatians get your class correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: It says "Warrant Officer Second Class Rajko Banduka," and my answer is the same as to the previous question. I was not there. I was not the one who established that communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was, sir, very simple: Were you a warrant officer second class on July 19th --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: On the 19th of July, I was not there in person. And, yes, I am Warrant Officer Second Class Rajko Banduka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that this conversation is -- from the Mladic perspective is very similar to the other conversation. And, again, you deny that this is you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6851, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why under seal? Mr. Registrar, in the list of the Prosecution it is not listed as under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey could you clarify if this has to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The boss tells me it doesn't. The Croatians didn't have some of the problems that we had with security with the other parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no need to have it under seal. Therefore admitted as a public exhibit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we note from both those last two intercepts that -- one of the main topics was the surrender, supposed surrender of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 25242.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting for that, did Zepa really surrender on the 19th or was that sort of a false alarm? From your own memory or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about either the date or this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We see that this is a report from the Republika Srpska SRNA Serbian press agency, and it's a public announcement from the information service of the VRS, dated 19 July 1995, 2000 hours, similar time as their intercepts and talks about the surrender of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6852, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, lastly, Mr. Banduka, you have said you were -- worked closely with General Mladic, you were aware of the communications systems. You may be aware that Serbian authorities several years ago searched General Mladic's house and they came up with audiotapes of conversations with General Mladic and others. And we have some of those audiotapes in this case, and on one of those audiotapes, a person, appearing to the Prosecution, introduces himself as Banduka and talks to someone named Nada. I can -- I'll play that tape briefly for you, if need be. But my question is: Were you -- tell us about your awareness of Mladic taping his own conversations? Did he have a system in place where he taped his own conversations on a tape recorder, a dictaphone or some other internal system as we've seen leaders do in the past, thinking of Richard Nixon, not to get him involved. But were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I had a dictaphone. I could use it to record conversations, but I never did for technical reasons. Because I would not have been able to present such conversations. So I don't remember any of those recorded conversations at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about your memory of them. Did they exist? Did Mladic do this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's play this and that this will be the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 01715A and we should see the appropriate part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. The way we've chosen to do it is to have the booth read the English while the transcript is being played, or while the tape is being played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If everyone is prepared to do it in this way, that it has been verified that what is heard is also what appears in the transcript, because that's the reason why we usually go in two rounds, the first one to verify the accuracy of the transcription and the second round to have that translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that and we can, of course, do that twice and the -- of course, the Defence has been provided with this material and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless the Defence now already agrees that the transcription is accurate. Because, in that situation, we would -- well, we still have a bit of a problem, because interpreters is not the same as translators and they're supposed not to translate written text but to interpret what they hear. So therefore I think the most -- is it a very long conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think the time we spent on how to deal with it takes even more time than it would do to play it twice. It will be played twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's about 45 seconds. The content is not what's the important part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed first round. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a digression, Your Honours. I did not notice that my learned friend Mr. McCloskey ever mentioned the date of this intercepted conversation. It was not recorded on -- in the transcript of today's hearing. However, before the hearing today, I was told when was that have -- supposed to happen. And I'm saying this for the benefit of the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we -- are you talking about the audio still to be played or any of the intercepts we looked at before?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one that we are supposed to be listening to in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what you intend to play is, according to the Prosecution, dated when?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not dated. It's, as the court may recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- we were provided a series of these audiotapes that came from Mladic's house so it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would not call it an intercept, though I can't discount the possibility that Mladic has got intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A recording of a telephone conversation. Let's listen to it the first time and we will not receive interpretation. Only in the second round we will. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Slobo: Yes. "Rajko Banduka: Banduka. Hello, Slobo. "Slobo: Hi. "Rajko Banduka: Is Nada with you by any chance? "Slobo: Yes, she just got in. "Rajko Banduka: Well, let me just ask her something. "Slobo: Okay, hold on. Nada. "Nada: Yes? Hello? "Rajko Banduka: Hi, Nada. Rajko here. "Nada: Hi. Tell me? "Rajko Banduka: Has the General arrived? "Nada: No "Rajko Banduka: Not yet? "Nada: No. "Rajko Banduka: Okay, thanks. "Nada: Somebody was just on the way driving up towards you. "Rajko Banduka: What -- some? "Nada: A car was coming, so I was wondering whether it was him. "Rajko Banduka: No, no, it wasn't. "Nada: It wasn't. "Rajko Banduka: Okay. "Nada: Okay. "Rajko Banduka: Take care. "Nada: Okay, bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise your -- introducing yourself on that right at the beginning of that little audio?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I never listened to my own voice. I wouldn't mind this being me. I wouldn't mind acknowledging the contents of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether you mind or not is not the issue. The issue is whether you recognise your voice. You say you never listened to your voice. Do you recognise the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember this conversation at all but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness, I think I invited him to continue his answer. He said he didn't remember the conversation but ... Would you tell us what said after that, or what you intended to say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to say that this conversation was quite possible. The date and the time are the things that I cannot define.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's see if you can help us. You're on the phone. You say: "Banduka." And then Slobo says something and you say: "Hello, Slobo." Slobo says: "Hi." You ask: "Is Nada with you by any chance?" So who would be talking to when you talked to Slobo and then asked Slobo if Nada is around?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I don't remember who Slobo could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Nada. Who's Nada?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Nada should have been General Tolimir's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And her last name is?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second, please. Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Finally, sir, now that you've had a chance to look at that, you've suggested it's something that could have happened. You've identified Nada. What is an audiotape like this doing in Mladic's house? You, better than anyone else, were close to him, from your own statement, and would know, in my view. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose it was his decision to take that tape with him. I didn't have a say in it, nor did I know that he had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know he was doing it, he was taping?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one clarification in relation to the last question. Earlier you said he was not taping. Now you say: "I did not know that he was taping." Do we have to understand your testimony that you were unaware of Mr. Mladic taping his own telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. It is possible that he always had this device with him, so he may have been taping other conversations and exchanges at meetings or elsewhere. I didn't know that he was doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that clarifies your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- could I ask just a clarification based on that answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, but shouldn't we then follow the usual order, that is, any matter triggered by questions by the Bench, that we'll deal with them last. First -- yes, Judge Fluegge has a question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One clarification to one answer you provided the Prosecution with. On page 16, you were asked: "Did Mladic and his command staff have the ability to move into the bunker and carry out -- and carry on the operations centre and communications from the bunker?" Your answer was: "Yes, that was possible. And that did happen during the bombing, that briefly we went to the command post." You were asked about the bunker. And you answered he went to the command post. And what about the question about the bunker? Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. You used the term "bunker." I don't know why I accepted the term for that facility. It was an underground facility as part of the Crna Rijeka. It was behind the villa on the outer side of the facility where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the question was if Mr. Mladic had the ability to move into the bunker during times when there were security concern, such as bombing. Was it used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have a few questions for you. You said you followed the events in Srebrenica and Zepa when you were in Bijeljina, and you followed it through the media. Could you tell us what media you were able to receive and what you learned from those media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I watched TV. At that time, only SRNA was accessible, the Serbian television, and I heard from the anchor about the event and I saw the images that were broadcast from the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the only channel you could receive on television, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Radio and/or written media, was there any foreign media available for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that time, I could not listen to any broadcast in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any questions, any further questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one to clarify a matter with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Banduka, you have a transcript of this conversation before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, it is P6852, just for the record, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Banduka, in this conversation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6853, Your Honours, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this conversation, do you see a record of General Mladic as one of the participants in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Banduka. I have no further questions for you, and I thank you kindly on behalf of the Mladic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, had you one question. Perhaps you have more now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned to the President that Mr. Mladic carried a device with him. Can you describe what that device was?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Well, it's a small dictaphone. The size is -- well, sort of something that people would keep in their pockets. Some people had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You picked up your glasses case. Is it -- what size is it in relation to your glasses case that we -- if you could show us, everybody, so we can see.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Roughly about this big. Like the glasses case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I think the record can reflect it's roughly the size of a typical glass case. I'm not great with centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the parties agree that usually - and I must admit I've used it for many, many, many years - that a dictaphone often is held in one hand and can be operated just by one hand. I see Mr. Stojanovic is nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we will agree on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, that doesn't say anything about what -- whether that was the same at the time, but at least that's a commonly used size dictaphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know, did that dictaphone use little tapes about the size of my creation here? If you know.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: Roughly, I think so. I think they're that big or smaller. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Mr. McCloskey puts in the air is something he fabricated with the size of approximately 3 to 4 centimetres by 1 and a half to 2 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions? It's [overlapping speakers] -- it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just asked by our client to put one question and it is based on the question that was put by Mr. McCloskey. With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the ordinary -- it's not the sequence because it's the cross-examining party who puts the last questions to the witness. But let me just consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very exceptionally -- and Mr. Mladic is hereby informed that if there's any question he would like counsel to put to the witness, that he should intervene at the moment when the last round, that is, re-examination, for the -- for the Defence is about to be concluded, rather than at any later stage. But exceptionally, Mr. Stojanovic, one question. And please be aware that if it triggers any need for the Prosecution, that they could put any question in relation to the same subject as well. And you know one question is not five but is one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Banduka, you were shown a photograph of the facility in Crna Rijeka. My question: Can you tell the Court which part of this facility was used by General Mladic for his own personal needs, in order to stay in that building?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO BANDUKA
utterances.text: The upper part, the upstairs. General Mladic and I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Typically your question could have been put in re-examination ... but Mr. Mladic should remain seated. Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic should remain seated. You know the rules, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Banduka, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, questions put by the parties, questions put by the Bench. I did understand that you have reasons to return as quickly as possible. I hope that we accommodated your travel programme, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, not your next witness, but is the next -- is the witness whose examination was interrupted ready to enter the courtroom? And I see that the usher already went out so, most likely, he will appear in a moment. Where we were, as a matter of fact, is that the examination-in-chief had been concluded and that Mr. Traldi was about to start his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rajak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony last Thursday. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You find him to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, now Exhibit D708, you say you were a member of the Territorial Defence of the Serb forces in the Rogatica municipality. Now, this Rogatica Serb TO was first organised in March 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And its commander was Rajko Kusic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Which company of the Territorial Defence were you in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And where was that company based?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was stationed to the south of Rogatica in the Kozici local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As of that time, when it was still the Territorial Defence, who was your commander in that company?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he remained your commander until you were injured in July 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you returned from your injuries in 1993 and joined the military police, who was your commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radenko Ilic was the name of the military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P3924.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a report by Mr. Kusic to the Drina Corps command dated 25 February 1993. We see it's identified as coming from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade in Rogatica. By February 1993, that what's the Rogatica Brigade was called; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page two in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see him describe - and it's just a few lines down in each language - "a group of SDS activists who returned to Rogatica municipality and volunteered to attend courses for anti-sabotage activities in education centres in Pazaric, Pancevo, and Han Pijesak, taught by patriotic JNA officers." Mr. Kusic writes: "That unit was the first organised formation of Serbian army in Rogatica municipality, and it was deployed on plateau Borika from the 3rd of March, 1992." What he's describing here is the beginning of the formation of the Rogatica Serb TO; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: A few lines below that, we read: "Unit from Borik, upon the invitation of the Serbian people from Visegrad, took part in salvation of Serbian people by entering into conflict with already established Ustasha formations." I have two questions for you about this. First, was it common in the Rogatica Brigade to refer to non-Serbs as Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, in paragraph 4 of your statement, you suggest that everyone in the Rogatica Serb TO was protecting their own home. In fact, the Rogatica Serb TO was also carrying out operations in other municipalities, like Visegrad; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that because I was up there in the Kozic local commune, so we did not receive all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you were not aware of what your commander, Mr. Kusic, is reporting to the Drina Corps here, that forces of the Rogatica Serb TO fought in Visegrad? You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we were ordinary soldiers. We could not know about every piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you, in your years as part of the Rogatica Veterans' Association, you've never heard that other fighters in the Serb TO and later in the brigade fought in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, I did find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you now know that the Rogatica Serb TO was, in fact, also carrying out operations in other municipalities, for instance, Visegrad; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since partly we have a border with the municipality of Visegrad, they went to defend our villages too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "our villages," you don't mean villages where people in the brigade lived. You mean Serb villages; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from the brigade that were from there too. But they're also Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, sir - and I'm done with this document - in paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that the Rogatica Brigade was formed in June of 1992. Now, I'm going to try to be very quick about this. On Thursday, at transcript page 27285, Mr. Lukic was summarising corrections to your statement and said about the Rogatica Brigade: "Until 22nd of May it was under TO, and after 22nd of May, 1992, it was army. That's how the witness" - meaning you - "sees it ..." Is it correct that your understanding is that as of the 22nd of May, 1992, the Rogatica Serb TO was incorporated into the Rogatica Brigade of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, just one correction. It was not Mr. Lukic but Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to correct myself. I think I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what happens if the examination of witnesses is interrupted, and -- but it's clear by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now -- I want to turn now my microphone on. And, after that, I want to turn to some of the corrections that you made to your statement with Mr. Lukic on Thursday. Now, you made changes to your statement regarding two facilities: The Vlahovic school and Rasadnik. Were you ever present at the Vlahovic school?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present there because physically we could not have been there since the entire town had been blocked by the Muslim forces, and we were to the south of the town of Rogatica, about 10 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "we," are you referring to your own company?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you do not know, then, from your own experience who the guards were there, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When I say "from your own experience," if you were never present there, you couldn't have any personal experience of who the guards were, could you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see for myself who the guards were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 9 of your statement -- actually, before we get to that. Were you ever present at Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never in Rasadnik either. For the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How did you come to learn that prisoners held in Rasadnik were exchanged in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the situation calmed down, I found out from my fellow combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you say you were never in Rasadnik either for the same reasons. In fact, when you returned in 1993 after your injuries, of course, Rogatica town was no longer being blocked and you could have gone to Rasadnik if you wanted to; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I had no need to do that and I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mention prisoners of war were detained there. Do you agree with me that civilians were also detained there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO RAJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just of Serb ethnicity. There were soldiers and prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you were asking about Rasadnik, isn't it? And, in paragraph 9, I read that -- oh, it has been changed. Yes. Yes, apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President I think we're fairly close to the break. I'd suggest we take it now. I think I have about 15 or 20 more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Traldi, if we could just clarify. You asked the question about civilians being also at -- in this detention place and the answer was: "Just of Serb ethnicity. There were soldiers and prisoners of war." I want to find out from the witness, when you say "just of Serb ethnicity," are you referring to civilians? Are you saying that the civilians were only of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, soldiers of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you said just -- oh, you're talking about soldiers. Then could you answer the question: Do you agree that civilians were also kept in that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I can continue, Your Honours, if you wish, but it is time for the break, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to clarify that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one question before we take the break. When you say you were not aware of any civilians, does that mean that you didn't know about civilians being detained in Rasadnik and also that you are not aware of any civilians detained in Vlahovic school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know about Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And about Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later. That it was a collection centre for all, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I might ask one follow-up question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
